locations.name: Gold Coast
locations.depot: Our own yard at 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, which sits at the top of the M1 run into the northern Gold Coast
locations.leadTime: Usually 2-4 business days between the order and the truck arriving
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where side access exists, in 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft and for anything lifted over a fence, a pool or a roofline
locations.metaDesc: Buy or hire a shipping container on the Gold Coast, run down the M1 from our Cornubia yard. Canal-block lifts and sandy ground sorted out first.
locations.line: Our yard is at Cornubia, which is effectively the top of the Gold Coast run, so the drive south is short and predictable and a truck can be on your street early in the day rather than late. That is the easy half. The other half is that the Coast hides some of the hardest suburban placements in the country behind some of its best addresses, and a waterfront lot with a metre and a half of side access is a crane job whether or not anybody has used the word yet.
locations.uses: site stores for the constant knockdown-rebuild work from Mermaid Beach up through Main Beach to Paradise Point, dry lock-up for surf clubs, dive shops and jet ski operators between seasons, parts and consumables storage across the industrial land at Yatala, Stapylton, Molendinar and Burleigh Heads, set and lighting storage for the production work around Oxenford, fit-out gear on the marine blocks at Coomera, and machinery, feed and tack on the hinterland acreage through Currumbin Valley, Tallebudgera and Mudgeeraba
access: Treat the Coast as three separate delivery problems. The first is the flat country in the north, from Ormeau and Pimpama through Yatala, Stapylton and Coomera. That is twenty-odd minutes from the yard, most of it is hardstand and wide entries, and a rigid truck can line up straight before the bed goes up. Those jobs get booked and done. The second is the waterfront stock, and it is the reason we ask so many questions before quoting. On the canal lots at Sorrento, Mermaid Waters, Clear Island Waters, Runaway Bay and out through Hope Island, the useful width of the block is at the water and the street end is pinched, the house occupies the full frontage, and the side gate is usually decorative. Those are lifts, not tilt drops. Whether a lift happens is decided by the street rather than by the container: the horizontal distance the boom has to cover, the height of everything in the flight path, whether there is a service line strung across your frontage, and whether the road is wide enough to set outriggers without closing it to traffic. Third is the ground. Between Coombabah and Kirra you are on beach sand sitting over a shallow water table, and dry sand carries almost no load. A loaded truck will find the bottom of a nature strip that looked as firm as a car park. Behind the beach, canal fill that went in forty years ago has consolidated and generally behaves; the freshly cut blocks up in the northern estates have not and do not. The hinterland is a vehicle question again. The climbs to Tamborine, Springbrook and up Currumbin Valley are narrow, hard against the bank in sections, low in the canopy and short on turning room. A 20ft goes up there without much drama. A 40ft gets talked through before anybody books a truck.

sections.h: Cornubia to the Coast is a short run
p: Most people selling containers into the Gold Coast are carting them from a depot on the far side of Brisbane, which puts the truck on the Gateway and through the city before it even reaches the M1. Our yard is at Cornubia, off the M1 south of Brisbane, so a Coast delivery is a short leg on a road the driver runs constantly. The practical benefits are the boring ones that matter on the day: a truck that arrives when we said it would, a booking that can be shuffled by a day without wrecking anybody's week, and a second trip that is an inconvenience rather than a disaster if a driveway turns out to be softer than it looked.

It also means coming to look at the container is realistic instead of theoretical. Cornubia is thirty to forty minutes up the motorway from most of the Coast, the units stand on hardstand, and you can open the doors, walk the floor, check the seals and the corner posts and pick the one you want rather than accepting whatever turns up. The yard is open Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday morning 8am to 12pm. Ring 1300 467 776 first so the unit you want to look at is standing somewhere you can get around it. If the drive does not suit, we can photograph the exact unit on request and send the images through before delivery.

sections.h: Getting it over the roof on a waterfront lot
p: A crane delivery is ordinary work on the Gold Coast, but it needs more detail up front than backing a tilt-tray down a driveway. The three numbers that matter are reach, height and standing room. Reach is the horizontal distance from where the truck can legally park to where the container has to land, and a crane loses capacity quickly as the boom goes out, so a box travelling twenty-five metres over a two-storey house is a substantially larger machine than the same box going ten metres over a side fence. Height is everything in the flight path: roofline, palms, a pergola, a pool enclosure, the neighbour's poinciana. Standing room is the street itself, because the outriggers need firm ground and a footprint wider than the truck.

None of that is hard to establish, and you can do most of it with a phone in five minutes. Stand at the front gate and photograph the house. Turn around and photograph the street, taking in the power and comms lines across the frontage. Then walk to the back and photograph the spot from the yard looking toward the road. Those three images tell us more than a page of description, they let us price the job properly the first time instead of twice, and they mean the machine that turns up is the one the job actually needs. Where a lift genuinely will not work, we would much rather tell you that at quote stage than have a truck sitting in your cul-de-sac with nowhere to go.

sections.h: Sand, salt and what sits under the corners
p: A container carries its entire weight through the four corner castings, and each casting concentrates that load onto a footprint about the size of a dinner plate. On coastal sand or thin turf over sand that load goes down, unevenly, and it does not come back up. The frame twists a little, the door end stops sitting square, and what was a one-hand door becomes a two-person job inside a season. An hour's work and a few lengths of hardwood or a set of concrete pads beneath the castings, levelled along the sides and across the diagonals, prevents the lot of it. That is done as part of the delivery wherever the site permits, so say at quote stage whether you are on sand, on fill or on a slab and the right materials travel with the container.

Getting the floor up off the ground matters more here than inland because the water table is shallow along the whole strip. A container sitting hard against damp sand never dries out underneath, and on a long-term store that is where the trouble begins, not on the roof. A hundred millimetres of clear air under it, grass kept down around the bottom rail and leaf litter swept off the roof a couple of times a year is the entire maintenance program. Salt air on its own does very little to a box that spent its working life crossing oceans. Wet leaves held against a roof panel and long kikuyu trapping moisture against the steel do plenty. For a unit that will live outdoors permanently in a coastal position, ask for cargo-worthy, which is inspected wind and watertight in the yard before dispatch. The grades page lays out what separates one grade from another so the choice is made with your eyes open.

faqs.q: Can you lift a container into a back yard on a canal block at Mermaid Waters or Hope Island?
faqs.a: Yes, and on most waterfront lots there is no other way in, since the house occupies the full width of the block. The machine sets up on the roadway, takes the container up over the roof and lowers it exactly where you want it standing. It comes down to reach, clearance, road width for the outriggers and whatever wires cross your frontage. Photograph the house from your gateway, the wires above it, and the yard looking back toward the road, and you will generally have an answer that same day.

faqs.q: Will a truck get up to Tamborine Mountain or Springbrook?
faqs.a: A 20ft on a tilt-tray goes up all of those roads regularly. A 40ft is a different conversation. The climbs are narrow, tightly cambered, hard against the rock in places, and there is mature canopy hanging low over the carriageway on the Currumbin Valley and Numinbah runs. Long vehicles also need somewhere real to turn at the top, which a lot of hinterland driveways do not have. Where the length genuinely matters, two 20ft placed end to end usually gets you more usable space and a far simpler delivery. Send the address and a photo from your gate looking back at the road.

faqs.q: Will a container sink into the sand on a Gold Coast block?
faqs.a: Placed directly onto sand or thin turf it will, because the entire weight of the unit lands on four small footprints. Pads or hardwood sleepers beneath the corner castings, levelled along the sides and diagonals, take care of that permanently and hold the underside clear of a shallow water table. Mention the ground when you enquire and the materials come up on the truck with the container, so it is set up properly on the day instead of becoming a job for your weekend.

faqs.q: Can I look at the container before it is delivered to the Gold Coast?
faqs.a: Yes. The yard is at 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, roughly thirty to forty minutes up the M1 from most Coast addresses, and the units sit on hardstand where the doors can be swung open and the floor and corner posts inspected properly. Ring first so the unit is accessible and somebody is free to take you through it. If the trip is not practical, we will photograph the exact unit on request and send it through before delivery, covering the door end, the corners, the roof and the floor inside.

locations.name: Sunshine Coast
locations.depot: Our Cornubia yard south of Brisbane, with stock also moving through our Gympie depot just north of the Coast
locations.leadTime: Usually 3-5 business days; range and hinterland drops are slotted into the run up the escarpment
locations.truck: Tilt-tray in 10ft and 20ft; crane for 40ft, canal-estate lots and anything that has to clear a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire across the Sunshine Coast, Caloundra to Noosa and up the range. Sand, salt air and tight estate streets allowed for.
locations.line: Two things decide a Sunshine Coast delivery and neither of them is the container: altitude and ground. Below the escarpment you are on sand over a shallow water table, threaded with canal estates and new subdivisions drawn for cars rather than trucks. Above it, the roads to Maleny, Montville and Mapleton set a hard limit on what can physically arrive. Sort out which of those you are dealing with before you order and a Coast delivery is a non-event. Leave it and you find out on the morning.
locations.uses: storage for the strawberry, ginger and macadamia growers around Chevallum, Palmview and Yandina, feed, tack and machinery on the hinterland acreage through Eumundi, Cooroy, Doonan and Belli Park, site stores on the estate builds at Aura, Baringa, Nirimba and Palmview, board, kayak and dive gear where the garage stopped coping years ago, stock for market and event traders working the Eumundi and coastal weekend circuit, and parts and materials storage for trades on the industrial land at Kunda Park, Warana and Coolum
access: Start above the escarpment, because that is where the hard limits sit. The Blackall Range climbs out of Landsborough, Palmwoods and Nambour are narrow, awkwardly cambered and full of bends a long rigid truck cannot straighten out. Some pitches have rock on one shoulder and fresh air on the other, several carry length and weight restrictions, and old fig and eucalypt canopy hangs across the carriageway at about four metres. A tilt-tray with a 20ft on the back handles all of that. A 40ft is not a given and on one or two of those roads the answer is simply no. Up top, ordinary rural constraints stack on as well: unsealed driveways with a pronounced crown, table drains waiting either side, gates hung off square to the road, and a turnaround at the house that needs to be genuinely truck-sized rather than hopeful. The red volcanic soil and decomposed granite up there bind beautifully in the dry and go slippery within the hour once rain arrives, and the wet lingers longer at altitude than it does at the beach. Below the escarpment it is sand and water. Golden Beach, Pelican Waters, Marcoola, Coolum, Peregian and most of the Noosa side sit on sand over a high water table. It looks solid and carries very little. The canal and lake lots at Pelican Waters, Minyama, Mooloolaba, Twin Waters and Noosa Waters add the waterfront problem: house across the full width, no usable side access, and the only way in is over the fence. The newer corridor estates have narrow carriageways, cars parked both sides, stormwater grates and service pits sitting exactly where a loaded rear axle wants to be, and fill that has not seen enough summers to settle.

sections.h: Above the escarpment, the road picks the container
p: For an address at Maleny, Montville, Flaxton, Mapleton or anywhere along the top, the opening question is not what you intend to store. It is what can physically get there. Those roads were surveyed for a much smaller class of vehicle and nothing about them has grown since. The dependable option on the range is a 20ft on a tilt-tray, and it covers the great bulk of what people up there need. Where forty feet of length is genuinely the requirement, we check whether the approach will take a longer vehicle, and if it will not, two 20ft placed end to end gives you the same floor area, an easier delivery and the option of splitting them up later.

There is nothing precious about that position. A vehicle that cannot get around a bend on a range road is reversing downhill with no shoulder to work with, and a container that will not clear the gate at the top has to be taken all the way back down. Either one writes off a day. A couple of minutes on a satellite image of the driveway and gate, plus a photograph taken from your gateway looking back down the road, heads off nearly all of it. If you are on top and not sure, ring 1300 467 776 and talk us through the approach. Between us we have driven enough of those climbs to know which ones present no problem and which want a different plan.

sections.h: Canal lots and streets drawn for cars
p: A waterfront block at Minyama, Pelican Waters or Noosa Waters is usually a lift rather than a drop. The house occupies the width of the lot, the side gate is decorative, and the only route to the back yard goes over the roof. Crane deliveries are routine, but they need three things settled in advance: how far the boom has to reach from the nearest legal standing position, what height the container has to clear, and whether the street gives enough room for outriggers without shutting it. Photos from the gate, from the yard looking back and one straight up at the service lines answer all three.

The newer estates on the corridor bring the opposite problem. Streets at Aura, Baringa and Palmview are narrow by design, kerbside parking eats what is left, and there is often exactly one position where the truck can set up, directly in front of your block. If two cars are in it, the delivery does not happen, because there is nowhere else within reach. The nature strip and kerb crossing are dotted with water meters, comms pits and stormwater grates built to be driven over by a car, not stopped on by twenty tonne. Give the neighbours an hour's notice, clear the frontage, and tell us at the quote if there is a pit or a grate in the crossing. That one hour of preparation is the difference between a delivery and a second attempt.

sections.h: Sand, salt and a box that has to last twenty years
p: Coastal sand drains superbly and carries badly, which is a bad combination for something that puts its whole weight through four corner castings. Straight onto sand, a container settles unevenly, the frame goes slightly out of square, and the doors start binding. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, levelled along the sides and checked diagonally, deal with that once and for all. Where there is any fall across the site, the doors want to be at the top of it so gravity is helping rather than hindering, and the floor wants clear air beneath it, which counts for more here than inland because the water table sits close to the surface all along the strip.

After that the upkeep is minimal and it is worth knowing what actually causes trouble. It is not the sea breeze. It is leaf litter sitting wet on a roof panel for months, and grass grown up against the bottom rail holding moisture against the steel. Run a broom over the roof twice a year, keep the base clear, and swing the doors open on a fine day occasionally to let condensation move out. That is the entire regime. Anything living outdoors permanently in salt air wants to be cargo-worthy, which is inspected wind and watertight in the yard before dispatch, and the grades page is worth reading first so the decision is an informed one rather than a price one.

faqs.q: Can you get a 40ft container up to Maleny, Montville or Mapleton?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and it is the road that decides rather than the box. Those climbs are narrow, tightly bent, restricted in places and low in the canopy, and a long vehicle under a 40ft cannot always negotiate them safely. On the range, a 20ft on a tilt-tray is the dependable choice. Where the length genuinely matters, two 20ft end to end will usually give you more workable space, more flexibility about where they sit, and a much simpler delivery. Send the address with photographs of the gateway and the driveway and you will get a straight answer on size before anything is booked.

faqs.q: My Pelican Waters block has no side access. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Yes, by craning it off the road and over the house into your back yard. That is normal practice on the canal and lake estates between Golden Beach and Noosa Waters, where houses run boundary to boundary. Feasibility rests on the reach required from wherever the machine can legally sit, the height of everything under the flight path, any services strung along the frontage, and whether the roadway allows outriggers to go down. Photograph the gateway, the yard and the wires above, and the job gets answered quickly and priced once.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to the Sunshine Coast take?
faqs.a: Three to five business days is the usual window, with coastal addresses at the quicker end. Anything above the escarpment gets grouped into a range run, so those can sit an extra day or two, and steady rain will push an unsealed-driveway drop back rather than putting a truck into soft ground on your property. Where the date cannot move, because of a settlement, a site start or removalists already locked in, say so when you enquire and the run gets built around it instead of you hearing afterwards that it did not fit.

faqs.q: Where does a Sunshine Coast container actually come from?
faqs.a: Either our yard at Cornubia, south of Brisbane, or our depot at Gympie just north of the Coast, depending on what you have asked for and what is standing where. Cornubia is the one you can walk into, Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday 8am to 12pm, and the containers there sit on hardstand where you can open the doors and inspect the floor and seals yourself. Inspection at Gympie is by arrangement, so ring first. If neither trip suits, we will photograph the exact unit on request and send it through before delivery.

locations.name: Ipswich
locations.depot: Our Cornubia yard, run straight through on the Logan Motorway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2-3 business days between the order and the container landing
locations.truck: Tilt-tray in 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft and for the older streets around the town centre
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Ipswich, delivered from our Cornubia yard. Old mine workings, river flats and new-estate streets accounted for.
locations.line: Ipswich sits on a hundred and fifty years of coal mining and in a fair few suburbs the old workings are still down there under the houses. That is not something anybody thinks about when they buy a shed, but a container puts its whole weight through four small footprints and where it goes matters. Add the Bremer and Brisbane River flats on one side and cracking clay on the other and the ground is the entire story here. The trucking to Ipswich is simple. The placement is where the thinking goes.
locations.uses: storage while a Woodend or Sadliers Crossing worker's cottage is restumped and reclad, dry lock-up on the estates at Ripley, South Ripley and Redbank Plains where the shed is still a line on a plan, trade and plant storage across the Carole Park, Wulkuraka and Swanbank industrial land, contractor gear for the work running around the base at Amberley, hay, fencing and machinery on the small holdings through Rosewood, Marburg and Grandchester, and stock overflow for businesses along the Brisbane Road corridor
access: Which part of Ipswich you are in changes the job completely. The growth corridor at Ripley, South Ripley, Deebing Heights, Springfield Lakes and Redbank Plains is estate country, and estate country has a repeating set of constraints. Carriageways are narrow, cars park both sides, and there is generally one position where a rigid truck can set up, which is directly in front of your block. The kerb crossings carry water meters, comms pits and stormwater grates designed to be driven across by a car rather than stopped on by a loaded rear axle, and cracking one turns into the property owner's problem rather than the driver's. Culs-de-sac turn tight for a vehicle with six metres hanging out past the back axle. The lots themselves have been cut and filled recently enough that the ground is still young, the turf over it is thin, and a corner casting will locate the soft spot on your behalf. The old town is the reverse. Woodend, Sadliers Crossing, Eastern Heights, North Ipswich and Booval have short pitched driveways, big camphor laurels and figs over the road, low service lines and side gates set out when a wheelbarrow was the widest thing going through them. Many of those are perfectly deliverable, just as a lift rather than a tilt drop. Then there is the ground itself, which splits three ways. West and south through Rosewood, Marburg, Willowbank and Amberley you get heavy reactive clay that is like concrete in spring and like grease in February. Along the Bremer and the Brisbane at Karalee, Barellan Point, Riverview and One Mile it is river silt and old alluvium that behaves the same way for different reasons. And through the old mining belt from Blackstone and Bundamba across to Collingwood Park, Dinmore, Tivoli and Ebbw Vale there are historic workings under the surface, which is rarely a delivery issue but is very much worth mentioning to us if your block has any known history.

sections.h: Old workings under newer houses
p: The West Moreton coalfield ran under a broad band of what is now suburban Ipswich, and the record of exactly where every tunnel went is better in some places than others. Most of the time this has nothing to do with a container. It becomes relevant when a block has a known subsidence history, when there is visible cracking or a dip in the yard, or when somebody wants a 40ft parked long-term over ground the owner already has doubts about. Our position is simple and it costs you nothing: tell us if there is any history, and we will place the container on the firmest and most stable part of the site rather than the most convenient one.

In practice that usually means moving it a few metres onto the driveway apron, a slab or a section of the block that has clearly been stable, rather than out in the middle of a lawn that has been quietly settling for a decade. It also means paying more attention than usual to what goes under the corners, because a properly pad-mounted container is far easier to check, re-level and lift out again later than one that has bedded itself into soft ground. None of this makes a container a bad idea in Ipswich. It just means the ten minutes spent choosing the spot is worth more here than almost anywhere else we deliver.

sections.h: On the flats, height is the only thing that protects anything
p: Ipswich floods, and people here carry the levels around in their heads more accurately than any web page could set them out. What deserves a blunt answer is what a container does and does not do. It keeps rain out from above. It is not a barrier. Once water rises to the level of the door sill it works past the seals, and an empty steel box of that size will lift and travel if it gets deep enough. Anyone telling you differently is selling something they should not be. Height is what protects the contents, and nothing else comes close to it.

That makes the worthwhile conversation one about siting rather than product. Choose the highest workable spot on the block ahead of the flattest one. Stay off the overland flow path, since a large share of the damage in recent events came from water sheeting across properties rather than the river rising into them. For a long-term store on low ground at Karalee, Barellan Point or One Mile, ask about lifting it further on blocks or a raised pad, keeping the floor well up and the underside dry and ventilated. Where the contents are genuinely irreplaceable, elevation is the most valuable decision available to you.

sections.h: Ripley, Springfield and the estate street problem
p: The corridor south and west of the town centre is one of the fastest-growing residential areas in the country, and most of the containers we put into Ipswich now go onto blocks that did not exist ten years ago. Those deliveries succeed or fail on one hour of preparation. Shift the cars off your frontage, warn the neighbours, and describe the kerb crossing to us, in particular whether a pit or a grate is set into it. If the frontage cannot be made to work at all, the fallback is a crane standing on the road and lifting over the fence. That is more machine than a tilt drop, and considerably less argument, and it lands first time.

The other estate question is size and it answers cleanly. On a lot of four to six hundred square metres, a 20ft is about the practical limit. Six metres of container wants nine or ten metres of straight approach to set down, which most driveways and side yards can produce. Go to 40ft and the side access is generally gone altogether, with something close to twenty metres of clear run needed, which those lots almost never offer. Where the shortage is volume rather than floor length, a 20ft high cube buys another 300mm of internal height over the same ground. Worth checking your covenant before you order, too, because a number of the estates out there are stricter than the council position and it is far cheaper to know first.

faqs.q: My Ipswich block is in an old mining area. Does that affect where a container can go?
faqs.a: It can, and it is worth raising with us at the enquiry rather than on delivery day. Old workings run under parts of Blackstone, Bundamba, Collingwood Park, Dinmore and Tivoli, and while the vast majority of jobs are entirely unaffected, we would rather site a container on the firmest, most stable part of a block than the most convenient. If you know of subsidence history, visible cracking or a dip in the yard, tell us. Mounting it properly on pads also means it can be checked, re-levelled or lifted out later without any drama.

faqs.q: Is a shipping container safe storage on a flood-prone Ipswich block?
faqs.a: It makes a very good store, though not because it holds floodwater out, since it does not. Water at door-sill level works past the seals, and an empty unit will lift and travel once it is deep enough. Elevation is what saves your contents. Choose the highest workable part of the block instead of the flattest one, stay out of the overland flow path, and give some thought to blocks or a raised pad that lifts the floor well up. Done that way it is an excellent long-term store. Relied on as a barrier, it will let you down at the worst possible moment.

faqs.q: Will a truck fit down my street at Ripley or Springfield Lakes?
faqs.a: Usually, given an hour of preparation. The same constraints repeat street after street: a narrow carriageway with cars along both kerbs, a single workable setup position immediately outside your block, service and stormwater lids in the crossing that break under a loaded rear axle, and a tight turning head. Clearing the parked cars off your frontage does most of the work. Photograph the street and the kerb crossing, send both through, and you will be told which truck is coming. Where the frontage cannot work at all, a lift over the fence can.

faqs.q: How quickly can you deliver to Ipswich, and can I see the container first?
faqs.a: Two to three business days is normal for a standard 20ft with clear access, and it is often quicker. What stretches it is a crane booking, wet weather on clay where waiting a day beats bogging a truck in your yard, or a unit needing a lockbox or vents fitted before it goes. The yard is at 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, straight through on the Logan Motorway, open Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday 8am to 12pm, and you are welcome to come and inspect. Ring first so the unit is accessible, or ask and we will photograph the exact one and send it to you before delivery.

locations.name: Logan
locations.depot: Our own yard at 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, which is inside the Logan City boundary
locations.leadTime: Often next business day, and rarely more than two
locations.truck: Tilt-tray in 10ft and 20ft; crane for 40ft and for estate frontages with nowhere to set up
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Logan, from our yard at Cornubia. Walk in, look at the actual unit, and have it on the ground tomorrow.
locations.line: The yard is in Logan. 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, with signage on the fence and containers standing in rows you can walk down. For a Logan delivery that means the cartage leg is fifteen or twenty minutes, a booking can be moved without it costing anybody a day, and you can come and inspect the exact unit you are buying instead of a photograph of one like it. What still takes planning is the far end, because Logan is seventy-odd suburbs and they do not deliver anything alike.
locations.uses: plant, tooling and consumables kept on the industrial estates at Crestmead, Berrinba, Slacks Creek and Meadowbrook, tools and materials for the trades working the estate builds at Yarrabilba and Logan Reserve, extra room on small lots where the garage went back to the cars, gear lock-up for footy, cricket and scout groups around Beenleigh and Browns Plains, stock overflow for small businesses working out of a home shed, and feed, tack and machinery on the rural-residential blocks at Chambers Flat, Munruben and Carbrook
access: The industrial half of Logan is some of the easiest work we do and there is no point pretending otherwise. The estates at Crestmead, Berrinba, Heathwood, Underwood, Slacks Creek and Meadowbrook were laid out for articulated vehicles, with broad entries and hardstand throughout. A container goes in there on a phone call and a gate code. The residential half is where the planning lives. Yarrabilba, Logan Reserve, Park Ridge, Flagstone and Greenbank repeat an identical set of problems street after street: a narrow carriageway with cars along both kerbs, one single position a rigid truck can work from which happens to be your frontage, comms and stormwater lids set into the crossing that will break under a loaded axle, and a turning head at the end of the cul-de-sac drawn around a garbage truck rather than something with six metres of container past the rear wheels. The blocks are cut and fill and eighteen months old, so the ground is still consolidating under thin turf. The older suburbs bring the opposite set. Woodridge, Kingston, Logan Central, Springwood, Daisy Hill and Shailer Park have short steep driveways that pitch away hard at the kerb, so a tilt bed grounds out before the container is clear, plus fifty years of gum and jacaranda over the road and side gates from an era of narrower mowers. A lot of those are lifts. Down on the river country at Eagleby, Bethania, Waterford and Loganholme the Logan and Albert flats are low, silty and slow to dry, and ground that looks firm on top can be soft two hundred millimetres down. Three photographs resolve nearly all of this: one along the street toward the house, one of the crossing and nature strip, and one of the intended position with whatever hangs above it in shot.

sections.h: Fifteen minutes from the yard
p: Being local is not a slogan here, it changes what we can do for you. A Logan address is a short run from Cornubia, which means next business day is genuinely normal rather than a best case, a delivery pushed by rain costs us a short trip rather than a full day of cartage, and if a container has to come back and be swapped for a different size or grade that is an inconvenience instead of an argument. Suppliers become flexible or inflexible depending on what a mistake costs them, and on a Logan job a mistake costs us very little.

It also means you can do the sensible thing and look before you buy. Come to 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, Monday to Friday between 7:30am and 5pm or Saturday morning 8am to 12pm, and walk the rows. Swing the doors, sight down the floor, look at the seals and the corner posts, and put your head inside to see what light comes through. That is a fifteen minute drive from most of Logan and it removes every argument that normally happens after delivery. Ring 1300 467 776 before you come so the units you are interested in are standing where you can get at them, and so somebody is free to take you through the differences between grades rather than leaving you guessing.

sections.h: One usable stretch of kerb
p: On a new-estate frontage there is typically a single position where the truck can legally stand and safely work, and it is directly in front of your block. If two neighbours' cars are in it the delivery does not happen, because there is nowhere else within reach and no way to come back at it from the other direction. The same applies if the only route onto the property crosses a comms pit or a stormwater grate, since those are engineered for a car rolling over them, not for twenty tonne stopping on top. Cracked lids become the property owner's bill, not the driver's, which is why we ask about the crossing before we book a truck rather than after.

So there are three things we need from you and none of them are hard. Where can the truck legally stand, what does it have to cross to get onto the block, and what is overhead: power, comms, a verandah roof, a mature gum with limbs at four metres. Give the neighbours an hour's notice and clear the frontage. Mention at quote stage whether a pit or a grate sits in the crossing. Where a frontage simply cannot be worked, the fallback is craning off the road and over your fence. It is a bigger machine on the day, and the container lands first time, which on a cramped estate street repays the difference easily.

sections.h: Low ground at Eagleby, Bethania and Waterford
p: The Logan and Albert river flats run through a good slice of the city and they behave differently from the ridges. The soil is silt and old alluvium, it lets water go slowly, and a block that reads as dry on top can still be soft two hundred millimetres down a week after decent rain. Put a container straight onto that and it settles unevenly. Every bit of the load runs through four castings, and the moment they are no longer at a common height the frame starts fighting itself, the door end twists, and doors that opened with one hand need a shoulder behind them.

Fixing it is cheap and it lasts. Four concrete pads or hardwood sleepers beneath the corner castings, bedded down, then checked for level along the sides and across both diagonals, with the doors at the top of any fall so they swing the easy way. Lift the floor a hundred millimetres or so clear of the dirt so air can move under there and the underside is not pressed against damp soil for the next decade. That levelling is done on delivery wherever the site permits, so mention at quote stage that the ground is low, soft or on a slope and the timber comes up on the truck. Give some thought as well to where the unit sits in relation to the drainage the builder designed, because six metres of steel dropped across a flow path pushes water somewhere the landscaper never intended.

faqs.q: Can I come and look at containers in Logan before I buy?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the simplest thing you can do. The yard is at 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, open Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday 8am to 12pm. The units stand on hardstand, so you can swing the doors, sight down the floor, look at the seals and work out for yourself what a grade actually means. Ring 1300 467 776 first so the units you want to see are accessible and somebody is free to walk you through them. If you cannot get in, we will photograph the exact unit on request and send it through before delivery.

faqs.q: Can a truck get into a street at Yarrabilba or Logan Reserve?
faqs.a: Usually, provided the frontage is clear on the day. Cars line both kerbs out there, and a tilt-tray needs one particular length of kerb directly outside your block to work from. Service lids and stormwater grates in the crossing are the other constraint, since a loaded rear axle will break them. Get the cars shifted for an hour, describe the crossing to us beforehand, and most of these run smoothly. If the frontage truly cannot be used, a lift from the road over your fence can, and it is frequently the faster way in regardless.

faqs.q: How fast can you get a container onto a site in Logan?
faqs.a: Next business day comes up regularly, since the yard is at Cornubia rather than the far side of Brisbane. A plain 20ft heading somewhere with open access is the quick end of it. Time gets added by a crane booking, a modification such as a lockbox or vents, or wet weather on soft ground, where waiting a day is better than a truck buried on your block. Where the date is fixed by a settlement, a site start or removalists already locked in, say so up front and the run gets built around it.

faqs.q: Does a container on a residential block in Logan need approval?
faqs.a: That turns on three things: how long it is there for, whether it can be seen from the road, and what it is being used for. A lot of the newer estates also carry covenants tighter than anything the council requires. Nobody here is going to guess at the rule covering your particular street, and it is worth establishing before you order rather than afterwards. The shape of it is predictable enough to plan around. Short-term, screened and used for storage sits at the easy end. Permanent, prominent and modified is where questions get asked. Moving one later means paying for a second delivery.

locations.name: Redlands
locations.depot: Our Cornubia yard, a short run over Mount Cotton Road into the shire
locations.leadTime: Usually 1-3 business days on the mainland; island jobs are arranged around the barge
locations.truck: Tilt-tray wherever there is a usable side access; crane for 40ft, small bayside blocks and over-fence work
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire across the Redlands, minutes from our Cornubia yard. Bayside ground, tight blocks and bay island barge runs.
locations.line: Cornubia is on the Redlands doorstep. Up over Mount Cotton Road and you are in the shire, which makes this one of the shortest runs we do and one of the simplest to move if the weather turns. The complications are all local. Ground that changes character between one street and the next, older bayside blocks with no way down the side of the house, and a set of inhabited islands where the last leg of the delivery goes across water rather than over bitumen.
locations.uses: boats, trailers, crab pots and dive gear put somewhere the garage stopped being able to hold, plant and stock for the nurseries, turf farms and landscaping outfits the shire runs on, materials staged ahead of a build on one of the bay islands, furniture and contents parked while a bayside cottage comes down and goes back up, equipment lock-ups for schools, sailing clubs and community groups at Cleveland and Wellington Point, and machinery and feed on the acreage around Mount Cotton, Sheldon and Redland Bay
access: Redlands ground changes over remarkably short distances and getting that right is most of the job. Through Victoria Point, Redland Bay, Thornlands and Wellington Point you strike sandy profiles that drain fast and carry poorly, and a loaded truck will sit its rear duals down into a nature strip that looked entirely solid from the footpath. Move a couple of streets inland toward the paperbark and melaleuca flats and the profile flips: low ground that holds water and stays greasy underneath long after the top has dried off. Neither type rules out a delivery. Both are worth establishing before a truck is standing on your lawn. Block sizes are modest through much of the shire, especially in the older bayside pockets at Cleveland, Ormiston, Birkdale and Thorneside. Houses were built hard against one boundary, side gates are narrow, and mature gums and figs carry limbs at precisely the height a raised tilt bed needs. Overhead services along the frontage are common too. On a good number of those blocks, craning the container over the fence is both quicker and safer than threading a tilt-tray between the house and the fence line, and it is what we will normally suggest. The newer estates at Thornlands and Redland Bay bring the familiar pattern of narrow streets, kerbside parking, pits in the crossing and fill that has not settled. Then the islands, which are their own category. Russell, Macleay, Lamb and Karragarra are reached from Weinam Creek, and North Stradbroke from Toondah Harbour, so the delivery carries a marine leg with its own constraints on vehicle length, weight and loading. Island roads are frequently unsealed, narrow and short on turning space, and island blocks are often sand. All of it is doable and we do it. It gets arranged rather than simply booked.

sections.h: Getting one onto Russell, Macleay, Lamb or Karragarra
p: Island jobs come up constantly in Redlands enquiries and the answer is yes, with a process attached to it. The unit is carted by road to the ramp and then goes across on a barge, and that water leg governs everything else about the delivery. Vehicle length and weight ceilings, how loading is handled and when the runs go are all set by the barge operator, and they are not ours to guarantee on somebody else's behalf. You will not find a timetable or a standing arrangement published on this page for exactly that reason. Those details shift, and a stale website costs you a wasted morning at a ramp.

What happens instead is that the water leg gets worked out with you and the operator while the quote is being put together, so what comes back to you is a single answer covering the container and getting it onto your block, not a price for the box and vagueness about everything after the ramp. In practical terms a 20ft is a great deal simpler to land on an island than a 40ft, and once island roads and typical island block sizes come into it that only becomes truer. Give us the island, the street, whether the driveway is sealed and how much room there is to turn at the far end, and you will get something you can plan around.

sections.h: Sand on one street, bog on the next
p: The working version of the Redlands ground problem is that a walk past the front fence tells you nothing. Sandy ground presents as firm and is not. Low-lying ground looks dry across the top and is saturated two hundred millimetres beneath. Either one will let a corner casting drop away inside a single season, and a unit that has gone out of square has doors that no longer line up, which turns a good store into a daily irritation. Both situations have the same cheap remedy: pads or hardwood sleepers beneath the four castings, bedded in and levelled along the sides and across the diagonals, spreading the point load rather than letting it punch through.

The water table is why this counts for more here than in most districts. A floor pressed against wet ground never gets an opportunity to dry out below, and on anything kept long-term that is where the deterioration begins, well before the roof gives anybody trouble. Raise it a hundred to a hundred and fifty millimetres, let air circulate underneath, and after ten years the difference is obvious, in the state of the underside and in how simply the unit can be picked up again if you sell up or rearrange the yard. Describe the ground when you enquire, whether it is sand, wet and low-lying, recent fill or an existing slab, and the right materials travel up with the container and the levelling is done on the day.

sections.h: No side access at Ormiston or Wellington Point
p: A lot of the older bayside housing was built close to one boundary with a side gate sized for a wheelbarrow, which rules out backing a tilt-tray down the side and rules in a crane truck lifting from the street. That is routine work and it is not a fallback, it is often the better option, because a lift goes in first time and does not risk taking out a fence, a downpipe or the neighbour's hedge on the way through. Three things settle it: the horizontal distance to be covered, the height needed to clear the roof and the trees, and whether the roadway has room for outriggers with power and comms wires accounted for. Photograph the house from your gateway, the yard looking back toward the road, and the wires overhead, and the job gets answered quickly and priced once instead of twice.

faqs.q: Do you deliver out to the bay islands and Straddie?
faqs.a: Yes. The unit is carted to the ramp by road, Weinam Creek for Russell, Macleay, Lamb and Karragarra or Toondah Harbour for Straddie, then goes over on a barge. Vehicle size, weight and loading windows are set by the barge operator, and that leg gets organised with them while your quote is being prepared, rather than pricing the road portion and leaving the water to you. Landing a 20ft on an island is far simpler than a 40ft, and once you are onto island roads that gap widens. Name the island and the street, and describe the block.

faqs.q: My place at Cleveland has nothing down the side. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Rarely, because a crane parked on the road will take the container over your fence or your roof and put it in the back yard. It is ordinary work on the older bayside blocks, where houses were built tight to one boundary. Whether it goes ahead depends on the reach required, the height to be cleared, any services running along your frontage, and whether the roadway allows outriggers to go down. Photograph the house from the gateway, the yard looking back toward the road, and the wires above, and you will have a firm answer shortly.

faqs.q: Will a container sink into sandy or boggy Redlands ground?
faqs.a: Set down directly onto sand, thin turf or wet low-lying ground it will drop away unevenly, because everything the unit weighs arrives through four small footprints. Pads or hardwood sleepers beneath the castings, bedded and levelled, sort that out for good and hold the floor above a shallow water table. Say what the ground is when you enquire, whether sand, wet and low, recent fill or a slab, and the materials come up on the truck so it is levelled on the day rather than left as a job for your weekend.

faqs.q: How quickly can you deliver to the Redlands, and can I inspect first?
faqs.a: One to three business days is normal on the mainland, because the yard at 51-55 Bromley Street, Cornubia is only a short run over Mount Cotton Road. Island jobs get arranged around the barge and take longer to line up. You are very welcome to come and look at the containers first, Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm or Saturday 8am to 12pm. Ring 1300 467 776 so the units are accessible. If the trip does not suit, we will photograph the exact unit on request and send it through before delivery.

locations.name: Jimboomba
locations.depot: Our Cornubia yard, out through Logan and down the Mount Lindesay Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2-4 business days; a wet week moves an unsealed-driveway drop rather than cancelling it
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for most acreage placements; crane truck where the gate, the grid or the turning room says otherwise
locations.metaDesc: Buy or hire a shipping container around Jimboomba. Acreage delivery planned properly, from cattle grids and gravel drives to horse paddocks.
locations.line: Nobody out this way is short of space, which is exactly why acreage deliveries look simple on paper and occasionally are not. There is no body corporate, no parked Corolla in the one spot the truck needs, and room to swing a rigid vehicle around twice. What there is instead is a private grid nobody can vouch for, four hundred metres of gravel that behaves entirely differently after rain, and a gate that measures narrower than it looks from the ute.
locations.uses: hay, chaff and pellets kept dry and away from vermin, tack, rugs and float gear stored properly instead of in a shed with a hole in the roof, side-by-sides, slashers and ride-ons locked up out of the weather, fencing wire, posts and strainers in one place rather than four, irrigation fittings and pump gear for the turf and produce blocks on the Logan River flats at North Maclean and Stockleigh, and tools and materials for owner-builders working a block where the house is still two years off
access: Grids come first, because they are the item most often forgotten and the one most likely to finish a delivery badly. Twenty-odd tonne of truck and container concentrates through two axles, and a great many private grids on the rural-residential blocks around Jimboomba, Cedar Grove and Woodhill were welded up by a previous owner from whatever rail was lying around the shed, with a ute and a float in mind. No plate, no rating, and generally nobody left on the place who remembers. Where a grid cannot be vouched for, there are three ways around it: come in through a side gate instead, land the container on solid ground close to the road so it can be walked in with a tractor at your convenience, or send a machine that can stand outside the grid and reach past it. All three of those work. Discovering the answer halfway across does not. Driveways are the next item. Six hundred metres of crushed rock with a crown on it and drains cut down both sides is a pleasant run through spring. Give it a week of rain and the crown turns greasy, the edges go soft, and a wheel that wanders off the centre line ends up in a drain and stops there. Long approaches also need a genuine turnaround at the house end, since a tilt-tray must be square to the ground before it can unload and nobody enjoys reversing that far in fading light. Then the property itself: gateways that measure up tighter than they appear, a service line to the pump shed strung at precisely the height a raised bed wants to occupy, ironbark limbs at four metres, and reactive clay that behaves like concrete in spring and like pudding in February. On the horse blocks this district is full of, there is also the plain fact that a steel box grinding down a steel bed is not a noise most horses have encountered.

sections.h: Nobody knows what the grid is rated to
p: Three bits of infrastructure settle most deliveries around here, and every one of them can be checked before you place an order. Start with the grid, where the truthful answer from most owners is that they have never known what it carries. That is fine, provided it gets said. The gateway is next. Measure across the opening at its tightest point rather than post to post, because the bed of the truck is wider than the container and a post already clipped once by a float will not survive being clipped by twenty tonne. Culverts are the third. Thirty-year-old pipe under a fill crossing, grass sprouting from the end of it and a dip forming in the surface above, is not something anyone wants to prove out with a loaded vehicle.

None of that rules out a delivery. It decides which vehicle turns up. Where the crossings or the approach are the sticking point, the usual solution is to land the unit on solid ground within reach of the road and leave you to walk it in with a tractor and chains whenever it suits, or to send a machine that can stand on firm going and reach past the soft part. The situation being avoided is a vehicle committed to an approach it has no way of backing out of, which turns twenty minutes of work into most of an afternoon and leaves a trench through your paddock as a souvenir.

sections.h: Four hundred metres of gravel, and what rain does to it
p: Unsealed driveways are the norm out here and most of them are perfectly good. What changes them is water. A formed-earth or gravel surface that has recently been graded has no bind in it at all and will not hold a loaded truck until traffic and a bit of weather have worked it. A crowned drive after a storm sheds water to the edges, which is exactly where the soft ground is, so a truck that comes off the centre line finds the table drain. Add any grade at all and a loaded vehicle loses traction long before an empty one would.

Rural bookings through the wet months therefore carry some deliberate give in them, and a call moving your date back two days beats committing a vehicle to an approach that has turned greasy. A bogged truck has no winners in it. You stand there watching it cut a trench and wondering who is paying for the tractor, and we have a driver and a vehicle tied up for the rest of the day. Your local knowledge is worth a lot here. You know whether your drive holds up or turns, which section goes first, and whether there is a hardstand near the shed or by the road that stays solid regardless. Tell us that at the booking and we will plan the run around it instead of guessing.

sections.h: Horses, dogs and gates that have to stay shut
p: This is horse country, and on an equestrian property the animals matter as much as the ground does. Unloading is a noisy business: hydraulics under load, chains running out, and a steel box grinding its way down a steel bed. Stock in a paddock the truck has to drive past, or horses standing in yards near where the container is going, want to be shifted before the vehicle arrives rather than after it is halfway down an approach with nowhere to turn around. Dogs take considerably more interest in a truck than is good for them. Say at the booking what animals are on the place, whether gates have to be closed behind us, and whether there is a preferred route in that keeps a truck clear of the arena or the laneway. It costs nothing to organise and it decides whether the whole thing takes a quiet twenty minutes or ruins the afternoon for everybody, horses included.

faqs.q: Is the grid on my driveway going to hold your truck?
faqs.a: The grid decides that, and out here most of them carry no plate and no paperwork at all. A truck under a loaded container puts far more through the rails than the ute and float it was probably welded up for. If yours was engineered and rated, say so. If nobody knows, say that instead, and the options become coming in through a side gate, landing the unit on solid ground near the road for you to walk in with the tractor, or sending a machine that reaches past the grid altogether. Any of those is better than rails folding mid-crossing.

faqs.q: Can you deliver down a long unsealed driveway?
faqs.a: Regularly, and through the dry months most are no trouble at all. The things that stop us are a surface gone slick after rain, cut drains a wheel can drop into, culverts of unknown condition, a recently graded surface that has not bound up yet, and no turnaround at the house end big enough for the vehicle. A tilt-tray has to sit square to unload, and it should not be backing several hundred metres out to the road. Photograph the drive from the gateway and the intended position from a few paces away, send both, and it can be planned properly.

faqs.q: What size container suits an acreage block out here?
faqs.a: Room is seldom the limiting factor, so it comes back to what is going inside and what your approach will take. A 20ft swallows feed, tack, fencing gear and a bench with space left over, and it is much easier to get through a gateway and down a drive. A 40ft gets you length enough for machinery and suits a working property with a decent run in off the road. Where the approach is awkward but the volume is needed, a pair of 20ft units stood a few metres apart with a roof spanning the gap is a popular and very practical arrangement out this way.

faqs.q: How do I stop it going out of square on clay ground?
faqs.a: Get it onto pads the day it lands. Clay through this district swells as it takes up water over a wet summer and shrinks back hard once the dry sets in, and it never does either evenly across a paddock. A unit sitting on bare soil tracks that movement one casting at a time and never recovers. Hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the four castings, dug in true and checked corner to corner, is the entire solution. Keep the doors at the top of any slope, the grass down, the underside clear, and it will still open cleanly in fifteen years.

locations.name: Beaudesert
locations.depot: Our Cornubia yard, run out along the Mount Lindesay Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2-4 business days, and we watch the crossings through the wet
locations.truck: Tilt-tray in 10ft and 20ft; crane truck wherever the approach or the yard leaves no room to sit square
locations.metaDesc: Containers for sale and hire across Beaudesert and the Scenic Rim, carted from our Cornubia yard. Causeways, gravel and working properties allowed for.
locations.line: Beaudesert town is a simple delivery and always has been. The interesting part starts once you turn off the highway, out toward Kooralbyn, Rathdowney, Christmas Creek, Laravale and the roads running up under Mount Barney, where a low-level causeway that was bone dry yesterday decides whether a truck comes today. Rain in the ranges puts water over crossings on properties where nobody saw a drop, and it can sit there for a day or two afterwards. Plan for that and it is easy country to deliver into.
locations.uses: fodder and baled hay held dry right through a wet summer, wire, posts and strainers locked away in one spot rather than four, handling gear, drenches and vet supplies kept out of the weather, chemicals and drums secured well away from the house, tools and machinery parts on places where the shed filled up years back, linen, furniture and equipment for the farm-stay and wedding venues dotted through the Scenic Rim, and dry storage while a shed or homestead is rebuilt after a storm has been through
access: What shapes deliveries out here more than anything else is the way water sits across roads. Tributaries of the Logan and the Albert thread through these properties, and where they meet a road it is usually a low concrete causeway rather than a bridge. Those come up within a couple of hours of a downpour in the ranges, frequently while it is still perfectly dry at your house, and they take their time going back down. Water over a causeway is not something a laden vehicle attempts, and that is physics rather than an excuse. Unsealed approaches are the second consideration. The back roads toward Christmas Creek, Innisplain, Palen Creek and behind Kooralbyn carry long gravel and formed-earth stretches that are superb in dry weather and treacherous within an hour of a storm, worst of all where a grader has been over them recently and nothing has worked the surface back together. Put a climb and a bit of side-slope under a laden vehicle and grip disappears far sooner than it would on an empty one. Ground on the properties themselves falls into two camps. The creek and river flats are alluvial, excellent when dry and slippery when not. Higher up you find basalt, loose scree and rock shelf beneath a shallow topsoil, which is about as solid as ground gets and almost never sits flat. Either way the unit belongs on pads instead of straight onto dirt. After that come the everyday farm details capable of halting a truck at the boundary: an opening that measures tighter than it looks, an unrated grid, cattle wandering the road or filling a laneway, a low span of wire to the pump shed, and a turning area at the far end big enough for the vehicle to square up before it unloads.

sections.h: The causeway decides the date
p: A phone call pushing your delivery back two days beats sending a laden vehicle at a rising causeway or down an approach that has turned to grease. That is not timidity. A truck caught on a causeway approach is a serious situation, and one buried on your property means a churned trench through the paddock, somebody's tractor, a disagreement over who wears the cost, and a driver and vehicle written off for the day. Rural bookings through the storm season carry deliberate slack for that reason, and you will get a call explaining the situation rather than an afternoon spent at the window watching for a vehicle that was never going to arrive.

Nothing available to us matches what you already know about your own approach. You know which crossing tips over first, how many hours it takes to fall away, and whether the gravel on your road firms up or turns to soup. Pass that on when the booking is made. Where there is a solid alternative, a sealed access through a neighbour, a hardstand near the boundary, a patch beside the shed that stays firm no matter what has fallen, it often decides whether the container arrives this week or next. Worth flagging too if the grader has recently been along your road, since a fresh surface has no cohesion in it at all and will not hold a laden vehicle until traffic and weather have worked it back together.

sections.h: Working properties, stock and where the truck turns
p: On a property being actively run, the delivery bends around the operation rather than the reverse. Gates that must be closed behind the truck. Cattle to be cleared from a laneway before anything drives down it. A grid nobody can vouch for at twenty tonne. A route in that steers well clear of the yards during weaning. Every one of those is straightforward when it comes up at booking time and every one of them is a headache once the truck is idling at your boundary. Worth knowing as well that the container can simply be set down on solid ground near the road, leaving you to walk it in with the tractor and chains whenever it suits. On a good many places around here that is the tidiest way to handle it and it spares everyone an ugly reverse.

sections.h: Setting one down on a slope
p: Hardly any ground in this district is flat, and a container has no need for flat ground. All it asks is that its four corners finish at one height. Across a slope, that means packing the downhill side up with stacked hardwood or pads set into the fall, not carving the uphill side away. Cutting in produces a shelf that collects run-off and holds it against the bottom rail. People get that the wrong way round constantly, and it separates a unit whose underside is still dry in twenty years from one sitting in a wet channel after every storm.

Set up correctly, the load runs through the castings exactly as the engineers intended, the frame holds true, and the doors swing sweetly for decades. Set up badly, the frame twists, the doors jam, and putting it right is a great deal more work than doing it properly would have been. Have the doors at the uphill end so gravity is on your side. Leave the underside open so air and water keep moving instead of pooling. Under trees, run a broom over the roof twice a year, because sodden leaf litter pressed against a panel does more harm than any amount of weather. That is the complete list of maintenance.

faqs.q: There is a causeway on the way into my place. Is that an issue?
faqs.a: Yes, so long as the causeway is clear and the ground each side of it is firm. Plenty of the crossings toward Christmas Creek, Laravale, Innisplain and out Rathdowney way rise within hours of rain up in the ranges and hold for a day or so afterwards, and no laden vehicle drives into water over a causeway. List the crossings on your route when you book and describe how they normally behave, and the run gets scheduled to suit. Failing that, the container can go down on solid ground near the road for you to bring in with the tractor later.

faqs.q: How much does wet weather affect delivery around Beaudesert?
faqs.a: Inside the town limits, hardly at all. Once you are onto gravel roads and long private approaches it matters enormously, since formed earth or a freshly graded surface turns slippery within the hour once a storm crosses, and grip goes out of a laden vehicle long before it goes out of an empty one. Expect a call moving the date rather than a truck sunk on your place. Rural runs through summer are planned with that flexibility built in from the start, and you get told what is happening instead of being left to guess.

faqs.q: Is a container any good for storing hay and feed out here?
faqs.a: It is one of the main reasons people around here buy one. It locks, birds and vermin stay outside, and cargo-worthy stock is inspected wind and watertight in the yard before dispatch, so feed that goes in dry comes out dry. Two habits make the difference. Stand it on pads, so air can move beneath it and the floor is not resting on damp ground. Then swing the doors open on a fine day every so often, letting any condensation clear instead of hanging around through a humid week. Have a look at the grades page before choosing.

faqs.q: How far out from Beaudesert will you deliver?
faqs.a: Right across the district. Kooralbyn, Rathdowney, Laravale, Gleneagle, Veresdale, Tamrookum, Christmas Creek, Innisplain and over toward Boonah and Canungra are all regular runs from our Cornubia yard along the Mount Lindesay Highway. The distance is rarely the problem out here, the last kilometre is. Give us the address plus a description of the approach, the crossings and what the turning space at the far end looks like, and the vehicle gets picked to suit before a quote is put together.

locations.name: Toowoomba
locations.depot: Our Cornubia yard, run west on the Warrego and up over the range
locations.leadTime: Usually 3-5 business days; range runs get grouped, so ring early if you have a fixed date
locations.truck: Tilt-tray in 10ft and 20ft; crane for 40ft, escarpment driveways and anything lifted over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Toowoomba and across the Darling Downs. Black soil, the range crossing and escarpment driveways handled properly.
locations.line: Everything about a Toowoomba job starts with the range. Seven hundred metres of altitude between our yard and your street, on a climb that has been the pinch point for heavy vehicles since trucks were invented, and a bypass that changed the equation for the better without making the old road irrelevant. Then you get to the top and meet black soil, which cracks wide enough in October to lose a fence post down and turns to grease in February. A container will sit on it happily for thirty years, provided somebody thinks about it on day one.
locations.uses: grain, seed and chemical storage on the farms out through Cambooya, Westbrook, Pittsworth and Oakey, parts and workshop storage for the mining and agricultural machinery trade around Torrington, Charlton and Wellcamp, site stores on the estate builds at Highfields, Glenvale and Kearneys Spring, secure storage for the constant renovation work on the old houses through East Toowoomba, Newtown and Rangeville, gear for the show, carnival and event circuit that runs through the city each year, and feed, tack and fencing on the small holdings toward Crows Nest, Hampton and Cabarlah
access: The climb is the first thing to understand and the bypass is the reason it is no longer the headache it once was. Heavy vehicles now have a graded route around the city that avoids dragging a loaded truck up the old range road through traffic, which makes a Toowoomba delivery more predictable and easier to schedule than it was a decade ago. It does not make it a short run. It is a couple of hours each way from Cornubia, so range work gets grouped and it pays to ring early if you have a date that cannot move. Once you are up, the city divides. West and south through Glenvale, Westbrook, Wilsonton, Harristown and Kearneys Spring the country is flat and open, the streets are wide, and a rigid truck has room to line up and unload without anybody breaking a sweat. East along the escarpment is a different job. Rangeville, Prince Henry Heights, Redwood, Mount Lofty and the streets running off the top of the range have short driveways that pitch away hard at the kerb, so a tilt bed grounds out before the container is clear, and the ground behind the house often falls away steeply toward the edge. Those are frequently crane jobs. The older streets through East Toowoomba and Newtown carry a hundred years of camphor laurel, jacaranda and plane tree at exactly truck height, along with low service lines and narrow side access. Out on the Downs proper the access is generally excellent, wide farm gates, hardstand near the sheds, and room to turn anywhere, with one caveat: black soil after rain is not something a loaded truck negotiates, it is something a loaded truck waits out. Frost is a genuine factor through winter as well, since a shaded driveway can hold ice well into the morning up here in a way it never does at sea level.

sections.h: Up the range, and why it pays to book early
p: Our containers come from the yard at Cornubia, which means a Toowoomba delivery is a proper run rather than a local drop. That is not a drawback, it just changes how it is scheduled. Range work gets grouped so trucks are not running half empty over the escarpment, which keeps the cartage sensible and makes the timing more predictable, and it means the useful thing you can do is tell us early. Where a settlement date, a shed coming down, a harvest window or a site start is driving the timing, say so up front and the range run gets built around you instead of an explanation arriving afterwards about why it did not fit.

It also means getting the specification right before the truck leaves matters more than it does on a suburban job. A wrong size or a missing lockbox on a Logan delivery is a short trip back. Over the range it is a day. So we ask more questions up front about what is going inside, how long for, what the site looks like and what will be opening the doors, and we would rather sort out a modification in the yard than discover the need for it at your gate. If you want to see a unit before it goes, Cornubia is open Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday 8am to 12pm. If the drive down the range is not worth making, we will photograph the exact unit on request and send it through before delivery.

sections.h: Black soil does not stay still
p: The vertosols across the Downs are some of the best cropping soil in the country and some of the least cooperative ground to park anything heavy on. They take up water and swell through a wet spell, then shrink and crack open through the dry, and they do not do either evenly across a paddock or a back yard. A container placed straight onto black soil follows that movement one corner at a time. It will not go back. Once the four corner castings stop sitting at the same height the frame carries its load unevenly, the door end racks, and doors that used to open with one hand need a shoulder and a bad word.

The fix is old fashioned and it works. Concrete pads or stacked hardwood sleepers under the four corner castings, bedded down onto firm material rather than sitting on the surface crust, checked level along both sides and both diagonals. Doors at the top of any slope so they open the easy way. Underside left open so water drains away and air keeps moving. Walk around it after the first solid wet and again after the first proper dry to see whether anything has shifted, because a unit re-levelled once in its first year will hold square for decades afterwards. That levelling is done on delivery wherever the site permits, so describe the ground at quote stage and the materials come up the range with the container.

sections.h: Escarpment blocks and the streets under the trees
p: Toowoomba has two very different kinds of hard delivery and they sit within a few kilometres of each other. The escarpment blocks along Rangeville, Redwood, Mount Lofty and Prince Henry Heights have short steep driveways, houses set high, and yards that fall away behind them toward the edge of the range. A tilt-tray grounds out at the kerb on a lot of those, and even where it gets in, the only usable ground is below the house rather than beside it. A crane truck lifting over the carport or the fence is usually the sensible answer, and it needs the same three photos any lift needs: the house from the street, the lines overhead, and the intended spot looking back toward the road.

The old streets through East Toowoomba, Newtown and the top of Ruthven are the other case. Mature camphor laurels, jacarandas and plane trees have been hanging over those roads for generations and the canopy sits at exactly the height a lifted tilt bed wants. Side gates were set out for narrower things. Service lines cross the frontage. Plenty of those blocks are perfectly deliverable with the right vehicle and a little notice, and a fair number are not tilt-tray sites at all. Give us the street and a photograph shot from out in the middle of the road facing the house, and the call can usually be made on the spot instead of guessed at.

faqs.q: Will a container stay level on black soil?
faqs.a: Only if you put it on something. Downs black soil swells when it is wet and cracks open when it is dry, and it does that unevenly across a site. Set straight onto the surface, a container settles corner by corner, goes out of square and starts binding its doors. Concrete pads or stacked hardwood sleepers under the four corner castings, bedded onto firm material and levelled on both diagonals, sorts it out. Check it once after the first big wet and once after a proper dry and re-level if anything has moved. Do that in the first year and it will stay square for decades.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a container to Toowoomba?
faqs.a: Three to five business days is the normal window. The containers come up from our yard at Cornubia, so range runs get grouped rather than sent one at a time, which keeps the cartage sensible but means a bit of notice helps. If you have a fixed date, a settlement, a harvest window, a shed coming down or a site start, tell us at the enquiry and we will schedule around it. Wet weather on black soil will move a farm delivery, because a loaded truck on soft Downs country is not a risk anybody should be taking.

faqs.q: Can you deliver out onto the Downs, not just into the city?
faqs.a: Yes, and the access out there is generally better than in town. Oakey, Pittsworth, Cambooya, Clifton, Crows Nest, Highfields, Jondaryan and further west are all serviceable, with wide gates, hardstand near the sheds and room to turn. The two things that change a farm delivery are the surface after rain and the last few hundred metres to the shed. Give us the address, tell us what the approach is like and whether there is somewhere firm to put the truck, and we will tell you what is coming and when.

faqs.q: My driveway in Rangeville is short and steep. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Often, though not with a tilt-tray. Where the driveway pitches away hard at the kerb, the bed touches down before the container has cleared it, and on the escarpment blocks the usable ground is frequently below or behind the house rather than beside it. A crane truck lifting over the carport or the fence is generally the answer. What decides it is reach, height clearance and whether the street gives room for outriggers. Send a photo from the middle of the road looking up at the house and one from the intended spot looking back and we can usually give you an answer straight away.
